Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always factor completely before canceling — never cancel terms, only factors.
  • Don’t forget to state domain restrictions after simplifying.
  • When adding or subtracting, the LCD must include all unique factors from each denominator.
  • Check for extraneous values that make any original denominator zero after simplifying.
  • Complex fractions simplify by multiplying top and bottom by the LCD of all small denominators.

unit: Unit 33: Graphing Rational Functions
description: Analyze and graph rational functions: identify vertical/horizontal/oblique asymptotes, holes, intercepts, and end behavior; use transformations and factor analysis to sketch accurate graphs.
content:
Definitions

  • Rational Function: A function of the form f(x)= p q where p, q are polynomials and q is not the zero polynomial.
  • Vertical Asymptote (VA): A vertical line x=a where f grows without bound as x approaches a; typically zeros of the denominator that do not cancel.
  • Horizontal Asymptote (HA): A horizontal line y=L describing end behavior as x goes to ±∞.
  • Oblique/Slant Asymptote: A non-horizontal line y=mx+b found by polynomial division when the numerator degree is exactly one more than the denominator degree.
  • Hole (Removable Discontinuity): A point removed from the graph caused by a common factor that cancels between numerator and denominator.

Key Concepts

  • Domain: All real x where the denominator is nonzero.
  • Intercepts: x-intercepts occur where the (simplified) numerator is zero and denominator is nonzero; the y-intercept is f(0) when defined.
  • End Behavior (degree test):
    • deg(p)<deg(q) ⇒ HA y=0.
    • deg(p)=deg(q) ⇒ HA at ratio of leading coefficients.
    • deg(p)=deg(q)+1 ⇒ slant asymptote from division. Higher differences ⇒ polynomial (nonlinear) asymptote.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  1. Factor numerator and denominator; identify and cancel common factors (note any holes).
  2. Domain: Exclude all values making the original denominator zero.
  3. Vertical Asymptotes: Remaining (non-canceled) zeros of the denominator.
  4. Horizontal/Slant Asymptote: Use degree test; if slant, perform polynomial division to find y=mx+b.
  5. Intercepts: x-intercepts from simplified numerator = 0 (and not at holes); y-intercept from f(0) if defined.
  6. Behavior near VAs: Test a value on each side to see if the function goes to +∞ or -∞.
  7. Sketch: Plot asymptotes, holes, intercepts, and a few test points in each region.

Example 1 — Simple Translation

Graph y= 1x-2 +3

  • VA: x=2; HA: y=3.
  • x-intercept: solve 0= 1x-2 +3 ⇒ 1+3(x-2)=0 ⇒ 3x-5=0 ⇒ x= 53 .
  • y-intercept: f(0)= 1-2+3= - 12 +3= 52 .

Example 2 — Slant Asymptote

Graph y= x2+1 x-1

  • Divide: x2+1 x-1 = x+1+ 2x-1 ⇒ slant asymptote y=x+1.
  • VA: x=1.
  • x-intercepts: solve x2+1=0 → none (no real roots). y-intercept: 1-1 is undefined ⇒ no y-intercept.

Example 3 — Hole and Horizontal Asymptote

Graph y= x2-1 x2-3x+2

  • Factor: numerator (x-1)(x+1); denominator (x-1)(x-2).
  • Cancel x-1 ⇒ hole at x=1. Reduced function x+1x-2 gives hole value 2-1=-2 ⇒ hole at (1,-2).
  • VA: x=2; HA (degrees equal) y=1.
  • x-intercept: from reduced numerator x+1=0 ⇒ x=-1 (valid). y-intercept: -1-2=12.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always analyze after canceling common factors; canceled factors create holes, not vertical asymptotes.
  • Intercepts must not lie at excluded domain values.
  • Horizontal asymptotes describe end behavior; the graph may cross an HA but never a VA.
  • For slant (or higher-degree) asymptotes, use polynomial division to get the asymptote equation.

unit: Unit 34: Solving Rational and Radical Equations and Inequalities
description: Solve equations and inequalities involving rational and radical expressions; identify and exclude extraneous solutions; express solutions in interval notation and justify using sign/interval testing or graphing.
content:
Definitions

  • Rational Equation: An equation that contains one or more rational expressions (fractions with polynomial numerators and denominators). Example: 3x−2=2.
  • Radical Equation: An equation that contains a variable inside a radical (root) symbol. Example: x+2=5.
  • Extraneous Solution: A value obtained when solving an equation that does not satisfy the original equation (often caused by squaring both sides or clearing denominators).
  • Rational Inequality: An inequality that involves rational expressions. Example: 1x−3>2.
  • Radical Inequality: An inequality involving a variable inside a radical. Example: x<4.

Key Concepts

  • Solving Rational Equations:
    • Identify all denominators and their restrictions (values that make denominators zero).
    • Find the least common denominator (LCD).
    • Multiply both sides of the equation by the LCD to eliminate denominators.
    • Solve the resulting polynomial equation.
    • Check all solutions in the original equation for restrictions or extraneous values.
  • Solving Radical Equations:
    • Isolate the radical term.
    • Raise both sides of the equation to the appropriate power to eliminate the radical.
    • Solve the resulting equation.
    • Check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation.
  • Solving Rational Inequalities:
    • Write the inequality so that one side equals zero.
    • Find the critical values (where the numerator or denominator equals zero).
    • Divide the number line into intervals based on the critical values.
    • Test each interval to determine the sign of the expression.
    • Write the solution in interval notation, excluding any points where the denominator is zero.
  • Solving Radical Inequalities:
    • Isolate the radical and consider domain restrictions (for even roots, the radicand must be nonnegative).
    • Square both sides carefully (if appropriate) to remove the radical.
    • Solve the resulting inequality and check solutions against domain restrictions.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  1. Rational Equations: Clear denominators → Solve simplified equation → Check for restrictions.
  2. Radical Equations: Isolate radical → Eliminate radical → Solve → Verify solutions.
  3. Rational Inequalities: Rewrite with 0 on one side → Find critical points → Test intervals → Exclude undefined values.
  4. Radical Inequalities: Determine domain → Square if necessary → Solve → Check and express solution intervals.

Example 1 — Solving a Rational Equation

Given: 2x−1+3=5x−1

  • LCD = x−1.
  • Multiply both sides by the LCD: 2+3(x−1)=5.
  • Simplify: 2+3x−3=5 → 3x=6.
  • Solution: x=2, with restriction x≠1.

Example 2 — Solving a Radical Equation

Given: x+1=x−1

  • Square both sides: x+1=(x−1)2.
  • Expand: x+1=x2−2x+1.
  • Rearrange: 0=x2−3x.
  • Factor: x(x−3)=0 → x=0 or x=3.
  • Check both in the original equation: only x=3 works.

Example 3 — Solving a Rational Inequality

Given: x+1x−2<0

  • Critical values: numerator = 0 at x=−1, denominator = 0 at x=2.
  • Test intervals: (−∞,−1), (−1,2), (2,∞).
  • Sign analysis gives solution (−1,2).

Example 4 — Solving a Radical Inequality

Given: x>x−2

  • Domain: x≥0.
  • Square both sides carefully: x>(x−2)2.
  • Expand: x>x2−4x+4 → 0>x2−5x+4.
  • Factor: (x−1)(x−4)<0 → Solution: 1<x<4.
  • Combine with domain: 1<x<4.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always find and state domain restrictions before solving rational equations.
  • When squaring both sides, always check for extraneous roots.
  • Never multiply or divide inequalities by an expression containing a variable unless you know its sign.
  • In rational inequalities, test sign changes only at critical points (numerator or denominator = 0).
  • For radical inequalities with even roots, ensure the radicand is nonnegative before solving.

unit: Unit 35: Inverse Functions
description: Determine and verify inverses algebraically and graphically (including restrictions to achieve one-to-one); use composition to check inverses; relate inverses of radical and simple rational functions via reflection across y = x.
content:
Definitions

  • Inverse Function: A function f-1 that “undoes” f, so that f∘f-1=I and f-1∘f=I (the identity function), when defined.
  • One-to-One (Injective): Each output corresponds to exactly one input; passes the Horizontal Line Test.
  • Reflection Property: The graphs of f and f-1 are mirror images across y=x.

Key Concepts

  • Existence: A function has an inverse (as a function) iff it is one-to-one on its domain (may require restricting the domain).
  • Notation: f-1 means the inverse function, not reciprocal.
  • Composition Check: For all x in the appropriate domains, f(f-1(x))=x and f-1(f(x))=x.

Step-by-Step: Finding an Inverse Algebraically

  1. Write y=f(x).
  2. Swap the roles of x and y: replace every y with x and every x with y.
  3. Solve the new equation for y.
  4. Rename the solved expression as f-1(x).
  5. State the correct domain and range (swap the original domain/range and apply any restrictions used).

Example 1 — Linear Function

Find the inverse of f(x)=3x-5.

  • Let y=3x-5. Swap: x=3y-5.
  • Solve for y: y=x+53.
  • Inverse: f-1(x)=x+53.

Example 2 — Rational Function (Solve & Restrict)

Find the inverse of f(x)=x-2x+1 (note domain excludes x=-1).

  • Let y=x-2x+1. Swap: x=y-2y+1.
  • Multiply: x(y+1)=y-2 ⇒ xy+x=y-2.
  • Group y-terms: xy-y=-x-2 ⇒ y(x-1)=-x-2.
  • Solve: y=-x-2x-1. Hence f-1(x)=-x-2x-1, with domain x≠1 (and original range excludes y=1).

Example 3 — Quadratic (Domain Restriction)

Find the inverse of f(x)=(x-2)2 by restricting the domain to x≥2 (to make it one-to-one).

  • y=(x-2)2. Swap: x=(y-2)2 (be careful—now solve for the old y).
  • Square root (choose the nonnegative branch due to the restriction): y-2=x ⇒ y=2+x.
  • Inverse: f-1(x)=2+x, with domain x≥0 and range y≥2.

Example 4 — Exponential/Log Pair

f(x)=ax with a>1 is one-to-one; inverse is f-1(x)=loga(x). Domains/ranges swap: exponential has domain all reals, range (0,∞); logarithm has domain (0,∞), range all reals.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Use the Horizontal Line Test to check if an inverse (as a function) exists; otherwise restrict the domain.
  • Don’t confuse f-1 with 1f; they are different ideas.
  • Always verify by composition and state appropriate domain/range after inversion.
  • Graphically, reflect points across the line y=x to move between a function and its inverse.

unit: Unit 36: Exponential Functions (Growth, Decay, Natural Base)
description: Explore exponential growth and decay models in the form y = a·b^x and y = a·e^(kx); identify key features such as initial value, rate of change, and asymptotes; interpret parameters in real-world contexts.
content:
Definitions

  • Exponential Function (discrete base): y=abx , where a is the initial value, b is the growth/decay factor, and b>0, b≠1.
  • Natural-Base Model (continuous): y=aekt (often written as y=aekt), where e is the natural base and k is the continuous growth (k>0) or decay (k<0) rate.
  • Percent Rate Model: If a quantity changes by r per period (as a decimal), then b=1+r (growth) or b=1-r (decay).
  • Doubling/Half-Life: Time to multiply by 2 or by 12 in a continuous model: td=ln⁡2k, t1/2=ln⁡2|k|.

Key Concepts

  • Growth vs. Decay: In y=abx, growth if b>1, decay if 0<b<1. In y=aekt, growth if k>0, decay if k<0.
  • Form Conversion: bx=eln⁡b⁢x. Thus y=abx=ae(ln⁡b)x with k=ln⁡b.
  • Asymptote & Intercepts: For a>0, horizontal asymptote y=0; y-intercept y=a at x=0.
  • Percentage to Factor: If a quantity increases by p% per period, b=1+p100. If it decreases by p%, b=1-p100.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Build a model from a percent rate:
    1. Write y=abx with b=1±r (sign by context).
    2. Use an initial condition (e.g., x=0) to find a.
  2. Convert to continuous form: Replace b with ek where k=ln⁡b, so y=aekx.
  3. Find k from two data points: With (t=0,y=a) and (t=T,y=Y), k=ln⁡YaT.
  4. Compute doubling/half-life (continuous): td=ln⁡2k, t1/2=ln⁡2|k|.

Examples

Example 1 — Percent Growth (discrete)

A population is 1,200 and grows 5% per year. Model after t years.

  • P(t)=1200(1+0.05)t or continuous form P(t)=1200ekt with k=ln⁡1.05.

Example 2 — Radioactive Decay (continuous)

A substance has half-life 24 days. Write Q(t) (days).

  • Use ekt1/2=12 ⇒ k=-ln⁡224. Then Q(t)=Q(0)e-ln⁡224t.

Example 3 — Find k from two measurements

A culture is 500 at t=0 and 800 after 6 hours. Model with y=aekt.

  • a=500, and 800=500ek⁢6 ⇒ k=ln⁡8005006. Model: y=500ekt.

Example 4 — Continuous Compounding (finance)

Amount after time t years at rate r (as decimal) with principal P:

  • A=Pert. For doubling time: td=ln⁡2r.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Keep bases positive: b>0, b≠1.
  • Do not confuse percent rate r with the factor b (use b=1±r).
  • When converting forms, use k=ln⁡b so that abx=aekx.
  • Asymptote y=0 is never crossed for a>0, but horizontal shifts or vertical translations (not covered here) can move it.

unit: Unit 37: Properties of Exponents
description: Apply and extend exponent rules (product, quotient, power, zero, negative, and fractional exponents) to simplify expressions and model relationships involving exponential patterns.
content:
Definitions

  • Exponential Expression: A form like an where a is the base (real, typically a>0) and n is the exponent (integer, rational, or real in advanced contexts).
  • Positive Integer Exponent: Repeated multiplication: an=a·a·…·a) (n factors).
  • Zero Exponent: For a≠0, a0=1.
  • Negative Exponent: Reciprocal power: a-n=1an (for a≠0).
  • Rational Exponent: For integers m, n with n>0: amn denotes anm (principal root when n is even and a≥0).

Key Properties (for bases where expressions are defined, typically a,b>0 and a,b≠0)

  • Product of Powers (same base): aman=am+n
  • Quotient of Powers (same base): aman=am-n, a ≠ 0
  • Power of a Power: amn=amn
  • Power of a Product: (ab)n=anbn
  • Power of a Quotient: (ab)n=anbn, b ≠ 0
  • Zero & Negative Exponents: a0=1;   a-n=1an
  • Rational Exponents ↔ Radicals: amn=anm=amn (when defined)
  • Like-Base Comparison (a>0, a≠1): If au=av, then u=v.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  1. Identify bases and exponents. Check domain (e.g., denominators ≠ 0; even roots have nonnegative radicands for real work).
  2. Apply product/quotient/power rules to combine or break down expressions.
  3. Rewrite negative exponents as reciprocals and rational exponents as radicals (or vice versa) to simplify.
  4. Collect like bases by adding/subtracting exponents when multiplying/dividing.
  5. Check form: express answers with positive exponents unless instructed otherwise; simplify numerical factors and radicals.

Example 1 — Simplify with Multiple Rules

Given: (xy)3x2

  • Power of a product: (xy)3=x3y3.
  • Divide by x2: x3x2y3=x1y3=xy3.

Example 2 — Negative & Fractional Exponents

Given: Simplify (8x)-23 (assume x>0).

  • Power of a quotient & negative exponent: (8x)-23=1(8x)23.
  • Compute the fractional power: (8x)23=823x23=832x23=22x23=4x23.
  • So the original is 14x23.

Example 3 — Solving by Equating Exponents

Given: Solve 53x−1=5x+5.

  • Same positive base (≠1), so set exponents equal: 3x−1=x+5.
  • Solve: 2x=6 → x=3.

Example 4 — Rewrite with Positive Exponents

Given: Simplify and write with positive exponents: a-3b-2.

  • Use negative-exponent rule: move factors across the fraction bar.
  • Result: b2a3.

Example 5 — Combine Like Bases

Given: Simplify x12x32 (assume x>0).

  • Add exponents: 12+32=2.
  • Result: x2.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Do not distribute exponents over sums/differences: (a+b)n ≠ an+bn in general.
  • Convert negative exponents to reciprocals to avoid sign mistakes.
  • When solving, equal bases let you equate exponents (for base a>0, a≠1).
  • With rational exponents and even denominators, mind principal roots and domain restrictions.
  • Keep final answers with positive exponents unless a problem specifies otherwise.

unit: Unit 38: Logarithms and Logarithmic Functions
description: Define logarithms as inverses of exponential functions; evaluate and interpret log expressions; graph logarithmic functions; identify domain, range, intercepts, and asymptotes; connect to real-world applications.
content:
Definitions

  • Logarithm (base b): For 1<b and x>0, logb(x) is the exponent to which b must be raised to get x; i.e., blogb(x)=x.
  • Natural Logarithm: ln(x) means loge(x), base e.
  • Inverse Relationship: Logs and exponentials are inverses: logb(bx)=x and blogb(x)=x.

Key Properties (for x>0, y>0, base b>1)

  • Product: logb(xy)=logb(x)+logb(y).
  • Quotient: logb(xy)=logb(x)-logb(y).
  • Power: logb(xr)=rlogb(x).
  • Change of Base: For any valid base k, logb(x)=logk(x)logk(b). Common choices: k=10 or e.
  • Domain/Range: For y=logb(x), domain (0,∞), range all real numbers; vertical asymptote at x=0.

Graph Features

  • Base b>1: increasing, passes through (1,0).
  • Base 0<b<1: decreasing, still through (1,0).
  • Transformations: y=alogb(x-h)+k shifts by h, k; vertical stretch/reflection by a; vertical asymptote at x=h.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Rewrite between forms: logb(x)=y iff by=x.
  2. Simplify using properties: expand or condense logs via product/quotient/power rules, ensuring all arguments remain positive.
  3. Solve logarithmic equations:
    1. Isolate the log (or logs) if possible.
    2. Convert to exponential form or combine into a single log.
    3. Solve the resulting algebraic equation.
    4. Check domain: discard any solutions that make log arguments nonpositive (extraneous solutions).

Examples

Example 1 — Change of Base

Rewrite log3(7) using natural logs.

log3(7)=ln(7)ln(3).

Example 2 — Expand and Condense

Expand ln(x3yz).

ln(x3yz)=ln(x3)+ln(y)-ln(z)=3ln(x)+ln(y)-ln(z).

Example 3 — Solve a Basic Log Equation

Solve log5(x)=3.

  • Convert: 53=x ⇒ x=125 (valid since x>0).

Example 4 — Solve with Multiple Logs

Solve ln(x-1)+ln(x+3)=ln(8).

  1. Combine: ln((x-1)(x+3))=ln(8).
  2. Drop logs: (x-1)(x+3)=8 ⇒ x2+2x-3=8 ⇒ x2+2x-11=0.
  3. Solve: x=-2±4+442=-2±482=-1±23.
  4. Check domain: need x>1 and x>-3 ⇒ only x=-1+23 is valid.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Arguments of logs must be positive; always check solutions against domain restrictions.
  • Do not split a log over addition/subtraction inside the argument: log(a+b) ≠ log(a)+log(b).
  • To solve, isolate a single log or condense multiple logs to one before converting to exponential form.
  • Base restrictions: use b>0, b≠1.

unit: Unit 39: Transformations of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
description: Analyze and apply transformations to exponential and logarithmic graphs, including translations, reflections, stretches, and compressions; describe effects of parameters a, b, h, and k in function form.
content:
Definitions

  • Parent Exponential: y=bx with b>0, b≠1. Domain: all real x; Range: (0,∞); Horizontal asymptote: y=0.
  • Parent Logarithmic: y=logbx (inverse of bx). Domain: (0,∞); Range: all real y; Vertical asymptote: x=0.
  • General Transformation (Exponential): y=Cba(x−h)+k.
  • General Transformation (Logarithmic): y=Clogba(x−h)+k.

Key Concepts

  • Vertical Shift: +k moves the graph up/down; shifts the asymptote: exponential asymptote y=k; logarithmic asymptote x=h unchanged by k.
  • Horizontal Shift: Replace x with x−h to move right by h (left if h negative). For logs, this also moves the vertical asymptote to x=h.
  • Vertical Stretch/Compression: Factor C scales y-values by |C|. If C<0, reflect across the x-axis.
  • Horizontal Stretch/Compression & Reflection: Factor a scales x-values by 1/|a|. If a<0, there is a reflection across the vertical line through the shift (exponential about x=h; logarithmic about its vertical asymptote x=h).
  • Domain/Range under Transformations:
    • Exponential y=Cba(x−h)+k: Domain = all real x; Range depends on sign of C: if C>0, then (k,∞); if C<0, then (−∞,k).
    • Logarithmic y=Clogba(x−h)+k: Domain given by a(x−h)>0 (so x>h if a>0, and x<h if a<0); Range = all real y.
  • Key Anchor Points:
    • Exponential: point at x=h becomes (h,C+k) (since exponent is 0).
    • Logarithmic: argument 1 gives log = 0, so a(x−h)=1 → anchor point (h+1a,k) (valid when this x lies in the domain).

Step-by-Step Procedure (Graphing)

  1. Identify parameters a, h, C, k, and base b.
  2. Shift the parent graph horizontally by h and vertically by k.
  3. Scale/Reflect using C (vertical) and a (horizontal).
  4. Update Asymptotes: exponential y=k; logarithmic x=h.
  5. Plot anchor points (exponential at (h,C+k); logarithmic at (h+1a,k)), then sketch respecting monotonicity (increasing if b>1, decreasing if 0<b<1).

Example 1 — Exponential Transformation

Given: y=23−(x−1)+4

  • Here b=3, a=−1 (reflection in x about x=1), h=1, C=2, k=4.
  • Asymptote: y=4.
  • Anchor at x=h: point (1,2+4)=(1,6).
  • Range: since C>0 but exponent has negative coefficient (horizontal reflection) only, the range is (4,∞).

Example 2 — Logarithmic Transformation (Vertical Reflection & Shift)

Given: y=−log212(x−6)+3

  • Parameters: C=−1 (reflect across x-axis), a=12 (horizontal stretch by factor 2), h=6, k=3.
  • Vertical asymptote: x=6.
  • Domain: require 12(x−6)>0 → x>6. Range: all real.
  • Anchor (argument = 1): set 12(x−6)=1 → x=8, yielding y=−0+3=3. So point (8,3).

Example 3 — Reading a Graph Rule from an Equation

Given: Determine transformations for y=−30.52(x+4)−1

  • Base 0.5 (decreasing). Horizontal factor a=2 (compress by 1/2), shift left 4 (h=−4), vertical stretch by 3 with reflection (C=−3), down 1 (k=−1).
  • Asymptote: y=−1; Anchor at x=−4: y=−3·1−1=−4.

Example 4 — Inverse Relationship

Given: The graph of y=2x−3+5. Sketch the inverse.

  • Inverse swaps x and y: solve x=2y−3+5 → x−5=2y−3 → log2x−5=y−3 → inverse is y=log2x−5+3.
  • As expected, the asymptotes switch: original y=5 ↔ inverse x=5.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Write transformations in the order: inside (horizontal) first, then outside (vertical). Track asymptotes after shifts.
  • For logs, always enforce the domain condition on the argument before graphing.
  • Horizontal reflections/compressions come from the coefficient of x inside; vertical ones come from the leading factor.
  • Exponential growth/decay depends on base: b>1 increases; 0<b<1 decreases.
  • Use anchor points: for exponentials, (h,C+k); for logs, the point where the argument equals 1 gives (h+1a,k).

unit: Unit 40: Properties of Logarithms
description: Use logarithmic properties (product, quotient, and power rules) to expand and condense expressions; apply change-of-base formula to evaluate logs and solve problems involving different bases.
content:
Definitions

  • Logarithm (base b): For b>0,b≠1 and x>0, logb(x) is the exponent y such that by=x.
  • Natural/Common Logs: ln(x) means base e; log(x) often means base 10 (context-dependent).

Fundamental Properties

  • Product Rule: logb(xy)=logb(x)+logb(y).
  • Quotient Rule: logb(xy)=logb(x)-logb(y).
  • Power Rule: logb(xr)=rlogb(x).
  • Inverse Identities: logb(bx)=x and blogb(x)=x.
  • Change of Base: For any valid base k, logb(x)=logk(x)logk(b).
  • Domain/Range: For y=logb(x), domain (0,∞), range all reals; vertical asymptote at x=0.

Expanding & Condensing

  • Expand: Use product/quotient/power to write a sum/difference of simpler logs.
  • Condense: Combine a sum/difference of logs (same base) into a single log by reversing the rules.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Expand only when arguments are products, quotients, or powers; keep arguments positive.
  2. Condense by moving coefficients inside as exponents, then product/quotient rules.
  3. Solve equations by isolating a single log and converting to exponential form, or by condensing multiple logs first; finally check the domain.

Examples

Example 1 — Expand

Expand ln(x4yz).

ln(x4yz) = ln(x4)+ln(y)-ln(z) = 4ln(x)+12ln(y)-ln(z)

Example 2 — Condense

Condense 2ln(a)-ln(b)+13ln(c).

ln(a2c13b)

Example 3 — Solve by Condensing

Solve log(x-1)+log(x-3)=log(4) (base 10).

  1. Condense: log((x-1)(x-3))=log(4).
  2. Drop logs: (x-1)(x-3)=4 ⇒ x2-4x+3=4 ⇒ x2-4x-1=0.
  3. Solve: x=4±16+42=2±5. Domain requires x>3, so the solution is x=2+5.

Example 4 — Change of Base (evaluate)

Express log3(7) using natural logs: ln(7)ln(3).

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Only apply log rules to products/quotients/powers inside a single log; never split over addition: log(a+b) is not equal to log(a)+log(b).
  • Check domain restrictions (argument>0) after solving; discard extraneous answers.
  • When changing base, choose k=e or k=10 for calculator evaluation.

unit: Unit 41: Solving Exponential and Logarithmic Equations
description: Solve exponential and logarithmic equations using inverse relationships, properties of logs, and appropriate algebraic techniques; check for extraneous solutions and interpret results in context.
content:
Definitions

  • Exponential Equation: An equation in which the variable appears in the exponent, e.g., ax=k with a>0, a≠1.
  • Logarithmic Equation: An equation involving logarithms of the variable, e.g., logbx−3=2 with b>0, b≠1.
  • Logarithm–Exponential Inverse: logbby=y and blogby=y for y>0.
  • Natural Logarithm: ln is log base e (where e≈2.71828).
  • Domain Condition for Logs: Any log argument must be positive: if logbR appears, then require R>0.

Key Concepts

  • Solving Exponential Equations:
    • Match bases when possible and equate exponents.
    • Otherwise, isolate the exponential part and apply a logarithm (often ln), then use log properties to solve for the variable.
    • Substitute when the equation is quadratic in form (e.g., let u=ax).
  • Solving Logarithmic Equations:
    • Combine logs using properties (product, quotient, power) into a single logarithm when possible.
    • Convert to exponential form to remove the logarithm.
    • Always check solutions against domain restrictions (arguments must be positive).
  • Log Properties (for u,v>0):
    • logbuv=logbu+logbv,   logbuv=logbu−logbv
    • logbur=rlogbu,   Change of base: logbu=lnulnb.
  • Checking Solutions: Clearing denominators or squaring, and taking exponentials/logs can introduce extraneous answers. Verify in the original equation, especially log domains.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  1. Identify the type (exponential or logarithmic) and isolate the exponential/log expression.
  2. Apply an inverse operation: take logs to bring down exponents, or convert a log equation to exponential form.
  3. Use properties (log rules or exponent rules) to solve for the variable.
  4. Simplify algebraically (collect terms, factor, or use substitution if quadratic in form).
  5. Check all candidate solutions in the original equation (domain/validity).

Example 1 — Exponential (Match Bases)

Solve: 32x−1=3x+5

  • Equal bases (3), equate exponents: 2x−1=x+5.
  • Solve: x=6.

Example 2 — Exponential (Use Natural Log)

Solve: 52x=17

  • Isolate the exponential: already isolated.
  • Take ln of both sides: ln52x=ln17.
  • Use log rules: ln5+xln2=ln17 → x=ln17−ln5ln2.

Example 3 — Exponential Quadratic in Form (Substitution)

Solve: e2x−5ex+6=0

  • Let u=ex (note u>0). Then u2−5u+6=0 → (u−2)(u−3)=0.
  • u=2 or u=3 → ex=2 or ex=3.
  • Hence x=ln2 or x=ln3.

Example 4 — Logarithmic (Combine and Exponentiate)

Solve: log3x−1+log3x−4=2

  • Domain: require x>4.
  • Product rule: log3(x−1)(x−4)=2.
  • Convert to exponential: (x−1)(x−4)=32=9.
  • Solve: x2−5x+4=9 → x2−5x−5=0.
  • Quadratic formula: x=5±25+202=5±452.
  • Only the value with x>4 is valid: x=5+352.

Example 5 — Logarithmic (Power Rule & Check)

Solve: 2log10x+1=log109(x−1)

  • Domain: x+1>0 and 9(x−1)>0 → x>1.
  • Power rule: log10x+12=log109(x−1) → arguments equal: x+12=9(x−1).
  • Expand/solve: x2+2x+1=9x−9 → x2−7x+10=0 → (x−5)(x−2)=0.
  • Solutions: x=2 or x=5. Both satisfy x>1, so both valid.

Example 6 — Mixed Bases (Take Logs)

Solve: 74x=35x

  • Take natural logs: ln7+xln4=ln3+xln5.
  • Group x-terms: x(ln4−ln5)=ln3−ln7.
  • x=ln3−ln7ln4−ln5.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Before solving log equations, write domain conditions (each argument > 0) and check final answers.
  • Do not distribute logs over addition/subtraction: logbu+v is not simplifiable by basic rules.
  • When isolating exponentials, factor/collect so a single exponential term remains before taking logs.
  • For forms like amx+p=bnx+q, taking logs and then grouping x-terms is efficient.
  • Use substitution when the equation is quadratic in ax or in a log expression.

unit: Unit 42: Modeling with Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
description: Apply exponential and logarithmic functions to model growth, decay, and real-world phenomena such as population, finance, and sound intensity; interpret parameters and compare model types.
content:
Definitions

  • Exponential Model (discrete-time): Quantity changes by a constant percentage per time step: y=Abt, where A is initial amount, b is growth/decay factor per period (b>1 growth, 0<b<1 decay).
  • Exponential (percent form): y=A(1+r)t, with rate r per period (negative for decay).
  • Continuous Exponential Model: y=Aekt, where k is continuous growth (k>0) or decay (k<0) rate.
  • Half-Life / Doubling Time: Time for a quantity to halve/double. For continuous models: T_half=ln2/|k|, T_double=ln2/k.
  • Logarithmic Model: Quantity changes quickly at first then slows: y=a+blnx (or y=a+blog10x), domain x>0.
  • Linearization (log transform): Taking logs of an exponential gives a line: lny=lnA+tlnb or lny=lnA+kt.

Key Concepts

  • Choosing a Model:
    • Constant relative change → exponential.
    • Rapid early change then leveling off without an upper bound → logarithmic.
    • Bounded growth toward a carrying capacity → logistic (beyond scope but useful context).
  • Parameter from Two Data Points: For times t_1, t_2 with values y_1, y_2 in y=Abt: b=y_2y_11t_2−t_1, and A=y_1bt_1.
  • Percent Rate vs. Factor: b=1+r (per time unit). Continuous rate relates by b=ek, so k=lnb.
  • Compounding: Interest after t years: periodic A(t)=P(1+rn)nt; continuous A(t)=Pert.
  • Units & Scaling: Ensure time units in r, k, and t match; log models require x>0.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Building a Model)

  1. Plot/inspect data to decide between exponential vs. logarithmic behavior.
  2. Choose form: y=Abt, y=Aekt, or y=a+blnx.
  3. Solve parameters from given points, rates, half-life/doubling time, or by linearizing (take logs and fit a line to lny vs. t).
  4. Check fit: verify with additional data points or residuals; confirm units and domains.
  5. Interpret parameters in context (initial value, growth/decay rate), and use the model to predict/answer questions.

Example 1 — Exponential Growth from Two Points

Given: A population is 120 at t=0 and 180 at t=3 years. Model P(t)=Abt.

  • A=120.
  • 180=120b3 → b3=32 → b=3213.
  • Model: P(t)=120(32)t3 or equivalently P=120ekt with k=ln3/2/3.

Example 2 — Radioactive Decay & Half-Life

Given: A substance has half-life 8 years, initial mass 50 g. Find mass after t years.

  • Use continuous model: M=50ekt with ek(8)=12 → k=−ln28.
  • Model: M(t)=50e−ln28t = 50(12)t8.

Example 3 — Finance: Continuous Compounding

Given: Deposit P=2000 at r=5% APR continuously compounded. Value after 6 years?

  • A(t)=Pert → A(6)=2000e0.05×6.

Example 4 — Logarithmic Model (Diminishing Returns)

Given: Learning score fits S=a+blnt. If S=40 at t=1 hr and S=55 at t=4 hrs, find a, b.

  • At t=1: 40=a+bln1 → a=40.
  • At t=4: 55=40+bln4 → b=15ln4.
  • Model: S=40+15ln4lnt, domain t>0.

Example 5 — Linearizing to Fit an Exponential

Given: Data appear exponential. To estimate A, k in y=Aekt:

  • Compute lny for each point and make a scatterplot vs. t.
  • Fit a line lny=mt+b; then k=m, A=eb.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Match units: if rate is per month, time must be in months (or convert).
  • Do not use log models with nonpositive inputs; ensure x>0.
  • For half-life/doubling, prefer k= formulas: k=ln2/T with appropriate sign.
  • When using two-point formulas, measure t from one of the data times (often set that time to 0) to simplify A.
  • Interpret parameters in context (initial value, rate) and report answers with units and sensible rounding.

unit: Unit 43: Arithmetic Sequences and Series
description: Define arithmetic sequences; find nth terms using explicit and recursive formulas; determine common difference; compute partial sums using Sₙ = n/2[2a₁ + (n−1)d]; apply sigma notation in context.
content:
Definitions

  • Arithmetic Sequence: A sequence where consecutive terms differ by a constant common difference d.
  • First Term: a1; the nth term is an.
  • Arithmetic Series: The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence, denoted Sn.

Key Formulas

  • Explicit (nth term): an = a1 + (n-1) d
  • Recursive: a1=a1 , an = an-1 + d (n≥2)
  • Between two terms: an = am + (n-m) d
  • Arithmetic Mean (one step): M = ak+ak+22
  • Sum of first n terms (two forms):
    • Sn = n2 (2a1+(n-1)d)
    • Sn = n2 (a1+an)
  • Sigma notation: Sn = ∑k=1 n ak

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Find the nth term given a1 and d:
    1. Use an=a1+(n-1)d.
  2. Find d from two terms am and an (n>m):
    1. d= an-am n-m
  3. Sum of first n terms:
    1. Find an (if needed).
    2. Use either sum formula for Sn.

Examples

Example 1 — nth Term

Given a1=7 and d=-3, find a15.

a15 = 7+ (15-1) (-3) = 7+14(-3) = 7-42=-35

Example 2 — Find d from Two Terms

Suppose a4=10 and a11=31. Find d and a1.

  • d= 31-1011-4 = 217 = 3
  • a4 = a1 + (4-1) d = a1 + 3(3) = a1+9 ⇒ a1=10-9=1.

Example 3 — Sum of First n Terms

Find S20 for the sequence with a1=5 and d=2.

  • First find a20=5+(20-1)(2)=43.
  • Then S20 = 202 (5+43) = 10⁢48 = 480

Example 4 — Sum with a Given Term

The 12th term is a12=50 and d=4. Find S12.

  • First term: a1 = a12 - (12-1) d = 50-11⁢4 = 6
  • Sum: S12 = 122 (a1+a12) = 6⁢(6+50) = 6⁢56 = 336

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Be careful with indexing: the factor is (n-1), not n, in the nth-term formula.
  • Use the two-term formula to avoid computing a1 when it’s not given.
  • For sums, either formula for Sn works; pick the one that fits your known values.
  • Check units and context: arithmetic sequences model linear growth/decline by constant increments.

unit: Unit 44: Geometric Sequences and Series
description: Define geometric sequences; find nth terms using explicit and recursive formulas; determine common ratio; compute partial sums using Sₙ = a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r) (r ≠ 1); use sigma notation and interpret applications.
content:
Definitions

  • Geometric Sequence: A sequence where each term after the first is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a constant common ratio r. If the first term is a1, then an=a1rn−1.
  • Recursive Form: For n≥2, an=ran−1 with given a1.
  • Geometric Series: The sum of terms of a geometric sequence. The partial sum of the first n terms is Sn.
  • Common Ratio: r=anan−1 (for an−1≠0).

Key Concepts

  • Explicit Formula (index starts at 1): an=a1rn−1.
  • Explicit Formula (index starts at 0): If first term is a0, then an=a0rn.
  • Finite Sum (r ≠ 1): Sn=a11−rn1−r.
  • Finite Sum (r = 1): Sn=na1.
  • Infinite Geometric Series: Converges iff |r|<1; sum is S∞=a11−r.
  • Solving for n: If an=a1rn−1, then for r>0, n=1+log(an/a1)log(r).
  • Geometric Mean (between a and b): The value g so that ga=bg, thus g=ab (for a,b≥0).

Step-by-Step Procedure

  1. Identify whether the sequence is geometric by checking the ratio between successive terms.
  2. Find parameters a1 (or a0) and r.
  3. Use the explicit or recursive form to get terms or to solve for a specific index.
  4. Compute sums using the finite-sum formula; for infinite sums, first verify |r|<1.
  5. Interpret results in context (growth/decay factor, alternating when r<0).

Example 1 — Identify and Write a Formula

Given: Sequence 5, 15, 45, 135, …

  • Common ratio: r=3, first term a1=5.
  • Explicit: an=53n−1.
  • Recursive: a1=5, an=3an−1.

Example 2 — Finite Sum

Find: S6 for the sequence in Example 1.

  • Sn=a11−rn1−r → S6=51−361−3.
  • Simplify: 51−729−2=57282=5·364=1820.

Example 3 — Infinite Sum

Given: Infinite series with a1=12 and r=14. Find S∞.

  • Since |r|<1, convergent.
  • S∞=121−14=1234=16.

Example 4 — Solve for n

Given: In a geometric sequence, a1=200, r=0.8. Find the smallest n such that an<50.

  • Set 2000.8n−1<50 → 0.8n−1<14.
  • Take logs (base > 1 or use natural log): n−1>log(14)log(0.8) (note both logs are negative).
  • Compute the inequality value and choose the least integer n satisfying it.

Example 5 — Word Problem (Savings Plan)

Scenario: You deposit $100 each month into an account earning 1% per month. The balance after n deposits is a geometric sum of grown deposits: Sn=1001.01n−11.01−1.

  • This is a finite geometric series with first grown term 100 and ratio 1.01.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Be consistent with indexing: confirm whether the first term is a0 or a1 before applying formulas.
  • For infinite sums, you must have |r|<1; otherwise the series diverges (no finite sum).
  • Negative r causes terms (and partial sums) to alternate in sign.
  • When solving for n using logs, mind inequality direction if the base/ratio is between 0 and 1.
  • To find r from two nonconsecutive terms ai and aj, use r=ajai1/(j−i).

unit: Unit 45: Recursive Formulas
description: Write and interpret recursive definitions for sequences (arithmetic, geometric, and other patterns); generate terms; translate between recursive and explicit forms when possible; model real situations recursively.
content:
Definitions

  • Sequence: An ordered list of numbers written as a1,a2,a3,… (or starting at index 0).
  • Recursive Formula: Defines each term using earlier term(s) and one or more initial conditions. Example: a1=3, an=an−1+2 for n≥2.
  • Initial Condition(s): Starting value(s) needed to begin the recursion (e.g., a1, or a0; for second-order recursions, two starting values).
  • Order of a Recurrence: The number of previous terms used (first-order uses an−1; second-order uses up to an−2).

Key Concepts

  • Arithmetic (recursive): Common difference d:
    • a1=A,   an=an−1+d for n≥2.
    • Equivalent explicit: an=A+d(n−1).
  • Geometric (recursive): Common ratio r:
    • a1=A,   an=ran−1.
    • Equivalent explicit: an=Arn−1.
  • Second-Order Linear Recurrence (constant coefficients): an=pan−1+qan−2 with two initial values. (Example: Fibonacci when p=q=1.)
  • Piecewise/Conditional Recursion: Rule depends on n or on the sign/size of previous terms (be sure to state each case and its starting index).
  • Indexing Matters: Always state whether the sequence starts at n=0 or n=1, and for which n your recursive rule applies.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Working with Recursive Formulas)

  1. Identify the order (how many previous terms are used) and list all initial conditions.
  2. Generate terms by iterating the rule carefully, keeping track of indices.
  3. Classify the type (arithmetic, geometric, linear second-order, or conditional).
  4. Convert to explicit when possible (arithmetic/geometric are straightforward; second-order may require more advanced methods or pattern recognition).
  5. Check your explicit formula by verifying it reproduces the first few recursive terms.

Example 1 — Arithmetic (Recursive → Terms → Explicit)

Given: a1=7,   an=an−1+4 for n≥2.

  • First terms: 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, …
  • Explicit: difference d=4 ⇒ an=7+4(n−1).

Example 2 — Geometric (Recursive → Terms → Explicit)

Given: a1=5,   an=1.2an−1.

  • First terms: 5, 6, 7.2, 8.64, …
  • Explicit: an=51.2n−1.

Example 3 — Second-Order (Fibonacci-Type)

Given: F1=1, F2=1,   Fn=Fn−1+Fn−2 for n≥3.

  • First terms: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …
  • Note: Requires two initial conditions since it uses two previous terms.

Example 4 — Piecewise Recursive Rule

Define: a1=2, and for n≥2:

an = { 2an−1+1 if an−1<10 an−1−3 if an−1≥10

  • Compute step-by-step, switching the rule when the condition changes.

Example 5 — Modeling with a First-Order Recurrence

Scenario: An account earns 1% per month and you deposit $100 at the end of each month. Let B0 be the starting balance.

  • Recursion: Bn=1.01Bn−1+100 for n≥1, with B0 given.
  • First terms found by iteration; a closed form exists but is beyond the current scope.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always state initial conditions clearly; without them, the recursion is incomplete.
  • Specify the index start and the domain of n for which the rule applies (e.g., "for n≥2").
  • Arithmetic vs. geometric: look for add a constant vs. multiply by a constant.
  • Second-order recursions need two starting values; check both are provided.
  • When converting to explicit, verify by plugging in small n to see if terms match.

unit: Unit 46: Sums of Infinite Series
description: Examine convergence of infinite geometric series (|r| < 1) and compute sums using S∞ = a₁/(1−r); recognize divergence when |r| ≥ 1; apply to financial and decay/growth contexts.
content:
Definitions

  • Series: The sum of the terms in a sequence.
  • Infinite Series: A series that continues indefinitely without an end.
  • Convergent Series: An infinite series that approaches a finite sum as the number of terms increases.
  • Divergent Series: An infinite series that does not approach a finite limit (the sum grows without bound or oscillates).

Key Concepts

  • For an infinite geometric series with first term a and common ratio r:
  • If |r|<1, the series converges and has a finite sum.
  • If |r|≥1, the series diverges (no finite sum exists).

Formula for the Sum of an Infinite Geometric Series

S= a1-r where |r|<1

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Identify the series and confirm it is geometric (each term multiplied by the same ratio).
  2. Find the first term a and common ratio r.
  3. Check if |r|<1 (required for convergence).
  4. If convergent, use S=a1-r to find the sum.
  5. If divergent, state that no finite sum exists.

Examples

Example 1 — Convergent Series

Find the sum of the series 5+2.5+1.25+0.625+….

  • Here, a=5 and r=12.
  • Since |r|<1, the series converges.
  • Sum: S= 51-12 = 512 = 10

Example 2 — Divergent Series

Determine if 3+6+12+24+… has a finite sum.

  • a=3, r=2.
  • |r|=2>1 → Divergent, no finite sum exists.

Example 3 — Application Problem

A ball is dropped from 10 meters and rebounds to 80% of its previous height each time. Find the total vertical distance it travels after infinite bounces.

  • Downward distance first: a=10.
  • Rebound heights form a geometric series: 10(0.8)+10(0.8)2+10(0.8)3+….
  • Each bounce adds two distances (up and down) except the first drop:
  • Total distance: D=10+2 10(0.8)1-0.8 = 10+2⁢80.2 = 10+80 = 90

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always test for convergence with |r|<1 before using the sum formula.
  • The formula S=a1-r applies only to infinite *geometric* series, not arithmetic or other types.
  • If r is negative, terms alternate in sign; check convergence carefully.
  • Real-world convergence examples include interest calculations, repeated decay, or diminishing returns.
